q: A bank's account and payment services are used only by its own mobile app; no outside party can build on them. A colleague calls this a platform. Do you agree?

items: **Engineering definition: fits** → a set of services that applications are built and run on
**Business definition: doesn't fit** → no outside parties build complementary products through its interfaces → **no ecosystem** yet
**Lecture expects both**: internal consumption **and** external complements
a.foot: To get there the bank would need **published, extensible interfaces** that partners can build against.

q: A company hosts its reusable services on a shared cluster but leaves service discovery, resource coordination and usage reporting to each application team. What is missing compared with the lecture's definition of a modern platform, and why does it matter?

items: **Modern platform** = both an **application architecture** and the **infrastructure** that hosts it
**Must solve itself**: discovery, resource coordination, orchestration and usage reporting
**Left to each team** → solved differently and repeatedly → the company is **sharing components**, not offering a platform
a.foot: Taking them on makes the **platform team responsible for infrastructure**, which is the work **platform engineering** exists to do.

q: A payments API is PCI-compliant and encrypts every transaction, but partners need three weeks of contracts and manual key exchange before their first test call, and there is no sandbox. Which platform characteristic is weakest, and what would you change?

items: **Why**: the on-ramp is slow and costly → discourages **producers and consumers** from joining
**Fix**: add **quick-start guides**, **code samples**, **self-service test credentials** and a **test card suite**, as **Google Pay** does
a.foot: **Security and compliance** should stay the default, so the **sandbox must not expose real card data**.

q: A platform team wants to replace its internal database and messaging stack. Dozens of partner apps call its published APIs. Which platform benefit lets the team do this without a partner release, and what would break it?

items: **Stable interfaces** → the inside evolves at its own pace without overly impacting the outside
**Breaks if** the change **leaks through the interface**, e.g. altering response fields or meanings
a.foot: Then the team needs a **new API version** and a **migration period** for partners.

q: A platform logs every transaction, but nobody analyses the logs and its service catalogue has not changed in two years. Which characteristic is it failing, and why is collecting data not enough?

a.lead: It is failing **stays relevant and data-driven**.
items: **Needs a feedback loop**: data **collected and then analysed** to improve the services
**Examples**: Google Pay's **analysis of spending**, **ML fraud detection**
**Logs nobody reads** support no decisions → the platform **drifts away** from what its users need

q: Your team adopts a toolkit that supplies abstract classes, dictates how the application is structured and calls your code at points it defines. A teammate calls it a library. Do you agree?

items: **Framework** = a **predefined skeleton** that **imposes a way of architecting** the application and supports certain **design patterns**
**Library** = code **you call** from your own application at points **you choose**
a.foot: A framework **shapes the whole design** → replacing it later costs **far more** than swapping a library.

q: An internal team announces 'we are building a platform', but its deliverable is a downloadable code skeleton that each app team installs and runs on its own servers. Is that a platform?

items: **Framework** can be **part of** a platform but is not one

sub: provides **hosted services** and **reusable components accessed by APIs**
lets applications **extend features** by **consuming and exposing services**
**collects data for analytics**

a.foot: To become a platform the team would need to **host and operate shared services**, not just distribute code.

q: A company's developers wait several days for an ops ticket to be approved before they get a test database. Which pain point is this, and what is the platform engineering answer?

items: **Pain point**: no **self-service** → developers **queue on operations** for routine provisioning

**Platform engineering answer**: replace the ticket with a **self-service capability** (a **portal**, **CLI** or **workload spec**) that provisions the database through an **automated, standardised workflow**
a.foot: The platform team must then **own and maintain that automation as a product**.

q: A CTO says: 'We already have a DevOps culture and an SRE team, so a platform team would be redundant.' Do you agree?

items: **DevOps**: **culture** and **CI/CD** with **shared responsibility**
**SRE**: applies software engineering to **reliability** through **SLOs**, **error budgets** and **toil reduction**
**Neither** builds an **internal developer platform** that treats **developers as customers** and offers **self-service golden paths**
a.foot: If the organisation has only **a few teams and services**, though, the **scale problem** a platform team solves may not exist yet.

q: Thirty application teams each maintain their own copied-and-edited pipeline scripts and infrastructure code. Which pain points does this show, and what would a platform offer?

items.t: **Pain points** (three of the top drivers in the survey):
sub: **no standardisation**
**lack of automation** through repeated manual work
**developer cognitive overload**

items: **Platform offers** a **golden path**: a supported, opinionated **pipeline and provisioning route** that every team can reuse
a.foot: **Cost**: less freedom for teams with unusual needs → the platform team has to **gather feedback** and **evolve the path**.

q: Six months after launch, a platform team wants to prove ROI and proposes reporting the number of portal logins per week. Does that metric show the platform's value?

items: **Logins measure activity**, not **delivery performance** → can rise simply because teams are **forced onto the portal**

items.t: **Use instead** → compare against the **baseline measured before launch**:
sub: **DORA metrics**: deployment frequency, lead time, MTTR, change failure rate
together with **developer NPS**

a.foot: Logins are useful only as a **secondary adoption signal**.

q: After a platform launch, deployment frequency rises but change failure rate also rises. Has the platform clearly improved delivery?

items: **Delivery is faster but less reliable** → the evidence is **mixed**
**Check** **lead time** and **MTTR** as well
**Look at** whether the **golden path** is missing **tests or guardrails** that teams used to apply by hand
**Developer feedback** shows whether the automation **reduces or just moves** the effort

q: In a GitOps setup, an engineer fixes a production configuration by editing the cluster directly. What happens next, and what should they have done?

items: **Git is the single source of truth** → the **CD tool** keeps **syncing the cluster to Git**
**Result** → overwrites the manual change, or leaves it as **unrecorded drift**
**Should have**: made the change through a **pull request** → **reviewed, versioned and reproducible**
a.foot: **GitOps trades** the speed of a direct edit for **auditability and repeatability**.

q: Developers on your platform currently write raw cluster manifests and infrastructure code for every service. A teammate proposes a workload spec in the developer control plane with an orchestrator behind it. What does this buy, and what does it cost?

items: **Developers declare WHAT** a workload needs (e.g. a database or a port) **without infrastructure knowledge**
**Orchestrator decides HOW** → generates **app and infrastructure configs** as a **resource graph** on each deployment
**Buys**: lower **cognitive load**; **standards and security** consistent across teams
a.foot: **Cost**: the platform team must **build and maintain the orchestrator rules**, and developers **lose direct control** of details.

q: A security lead proposes one security scan as the final stage before production. Where does the reference architecture put security, and why does that matter?

items: **Security is a cross-cutting plane**, **embedded everywhere**
**Secrets management**, **identity**, **access control**, **policies** and **compliance** apply to **every plane**, not just the last step
**A single final gate** → finds problems **late** and leaves **secrets and access** in earlier stages **unmanaged**
a.foot: Embedding it costs more **platform work up front** but makes **the secure path the default**.

q: A developer's workload spec is accepted, but the service fails in staging because no database exists there. Using the planes, where would you look first?

items: **Orchestrator** (in the **integration and delivery plane**) → turns the spec into a **resource graph for each environment**
**Resource plane** → **provisions** what that graph asks for
**Check first**: does the **staging resource graph** include the database, and did **provisioning run**?
**Observability plane** → should give **logs from every plane**
a.foot: This shows why **cross-cutting monitoring** matters.

q: A data science team wants to train and deploy models through the existing IDP. What does the reference model add for them, and why is the resource plane alone not enough?

items.t: **Adds the data and model management plane**:
sub: **feature engineering**, **experiment tracking**, **metadata**, **lineage** and a **model registry**
covers the **ML lifecycle** up to **production governance**

items: **Resource plane alone** → can supply **GPU nodes**, but doesn't track which **data and experiment** produced which **model**
a.foot: Without that plane the platform can **run** ML workloads but cannot **govern** them.

q: A platform team's first deliverable is a polished developer portal, while provisioning behind it is still done by ticket. Do you support the plan?

items: **Backend before portal** (the lecture's principle): a portal is **only an interface**
**Ticket-driven provisioning behind it** → nothing **self-service** happens
**Build first** the automation for the **top pain**: typically **CI/CD and IaC**, **golden paths** and an **orchestrator**
**Then** put a **portal or CLI** on top
a.foot: A portal can come early only as a **thin front** for automation that **already works**.

q: A security lead wants every developer to run three extra scanning tools by hand before each merge. Is this shifting left or shifting down, and what would you suggest?

items: **Shifting left**: moves checks **earlier** but **dumps the toil on developers**
**Shifting down**: embed the scans in the platform as **automated guardrails** and **secure defaults** on the **golden path** → the **safe route is also the easiest**
a.foot: The checks can still run early; what changes is **who does the work**.

q: A platform team plans an 18-month build covering every plane before any application team uses it. What would you change?

a.lead: Start with a **minimum viable platform** that solves the **most costly pain**, then expand.
items: **Long build with no users** → **delays value** and gets **no feedback** → the team may **build the wrong things**
Goes against the **'treat it as a product'** principle
**Measure from day one** → each step's impact is visible

q: A maturity survey shows most organisations stuck at 'Operational', with measurement the weakest dimension. Your new platform team has no baseline numbers. What do you do first, and why?

items: **Do first**: document the **current cost of the pain** (e.g. **ticket wait times**, **lead time**, **failure rates**) **before building anything**
**Why**: a platform is a **product that must prove ROI**
**No baseline** → no later **DORA** or **NPS** figure can show improvement
a.foot: Cheap to do **at the start**; almost **impossible to reconstruct later**.

q: A video site runs separate marketing budgets for creators and for viewers, treating them as two markets. What does 'think roles not markets' suggest instead?

items: **Users can play both roles** → viewers can become creators
**Magnet strategy** → converts **consumers into producers** over time
**Benefit** → saves **marketing spend** and **scales production of seeds**
a.foot: So invest in **lowering the barrier to producing** (e.g. **simple upload tools**) rather than buying **two separate audiences**.

q: A tutoring marketplace has plenty of registered tutors, but students complain that matches are poor and some tutors are low quality. Which platform component is weak, and what would you build?

a.lead: The **matchmaker**, not the magnet: supply exists, but **matching and curation** fail.
items: **Matching accuracy** → improve it to cut **false positives**
**Curate** tutors using **ratings and reviews**
**Trust mechanisms**
**ML** applied to matching
a.foot: In engineering terms: **curation components** and **matching algorithms**.

q: A furniture maker sells only its own products through its web shop and calls itself a platform because the shop has a public API. Is this a linear or a network business?

items: **Linear** → focus is the **process of production, assembly and distribution** of its **own goods**
**Network business** → focuses on **enabling interactions** between **independent producers and consumers**
**Technology is only an enabler** (lecture) → an **API alone does not make a platform**
a.foot: It would move towards a **network model** if **other makers** could list and sell through it.

q: A start-up wants to launch professional networking, messaging, job listings and content publishing all at once. What does the LinkedIn example advise?

items.t: **LinkedIn** started with **professional-to-professional connections**, each step **building adoption before monetisation**:
sub: then **discussions**, **recruiters** and **job seekers**
later **thought-leader content**

items: **Launching everything at once** → spreads the **magnet** thin → **too few producers** for any single interaction

q: Partners praise a platform's matching algorithm but say its SDK is confusing and integration takes weeks. Which platform aspect is weak, and which engineering concerns does it map to?

items: **Toolbox** = the **tools producers and consumers use to interact**
**Engineering concerns**: **service usability design**, **SDK and API design**, **integration with other services**
a.foot: A strong **matchmaker** cannot make up for a toolbox that **keeps partners from joining**.

q: Hundreds of third-party apps now depend on a platform's interfaces. A product manager proposes putting all of this quarter's effort into new features and deferring availability and security work. Do you agree?

items: **Architecting for the ecosystem** = **availability**, **security** and **scalability**
**Why** → an **outage or breach** now hits **every complement** built on the platform, not just one app
**Features still matter** for **growth**
a.foot: So the answer depends on whether **current availability and security** already meet **partners' needs**.

q: A platform plans to add a new kind of interaction every quarter, as the sample paper's ecosystem-growth question describes. Which engineering aspect must the design support, and what goes wrong without it?

items: **Needs** → **modular, extensible components** and an **agile architecture** for **scaling the platform business**
**Each new interaction** → plugs in as **new services** that **reuse existing domain entities and interfaces**
**Without it** → every addition means **changing the core** → each release **slows down** and risks **breaking existing interactions**

q: A food-delivery company wants to open its ordering, delivery-tracking and payment capabilities to independent restaurants and couriers. (a) Identify the seed, producers, consumers and core interaction. (b) The CEO wants to launch restaurant booking, grocery delivery and a courier marketplace in the same release. Advise. (c) Give two engineering concerns that follow from opening the APIs to outside parties.

sub: **Seed**: a **menu item** or **order**
**Producers**: **restaurants** and **couriers**
**Consumers**: **diners**
**Interaction**: browse, order, match a courier, deliver, pay

items.t: **(b) Build one interaction at a time**, as **LinkedIn** did
sub: Get **food ordering** adopted and **growing producers** through the **magnet** before adding new interactions
Design **modular, extensible components** so later ones **plug in**
**Toolbox** → needs **usable APIs and SDKs**
**Many outside parties** now depend on the platform → architect for **availability**, **security** and **scalability**

a.foot: **Trade-off**: slower initial scope in exchange for a **stable core**.

q: A company with 40 application teams has a five-day ticket wait for databases, each team maintains its own pipeline scripts, and leadership wants evidence of value within six months. Propose the first steps of an IDP, the measures you would use, and one thing you would deliberately not build first.

items.t: **Baseline first**: document the **cost of the pain**
sub: **ticket wait**, **lead time**, **failure rates**

items.t: **Minimum viable platform** aimed at the **top pain**
sub: **automated database provisioning** through **IaC**
a shared **CI/CD golden path**
an **orchestrator** or **pipeline** behind it

items.t: **Measures**: **DORA metrics** and **developer NPS** against the baseline
sub: **expand scope** only where they improve
**backend comes before portal**
a portal over **ticket-driven provisioning** would show nothing in **six months**

q: On an IDP, developers submit workload specs. Staging deployments work, but production sometimes gets a different database size and nobody can explain why. Using the reference architecture and GitOps, diagnose where to look and what to change.

items.t: **Look at the orchestrator** (**integration and delivery plane**)
sub: it generates **environment-specific configuration** as a **resource graph**
→ compare the **production and staging graphs** and the **rules** that produce them

items.t: **Check GitOps**: was production state **changed outside Git**?
sub: **Git** should be the **single source of truth**
every **infra change** should go through a **reviewed PR**

items: **Fix**: move **environment differences** into **versioned config** and let **CD sync from Git**
**Observability plane** → should **record what was deployed**, so the next difference is visible without detective work

q: An organisation with 300 developers has a DevOps culture and an SRE team that owns SLOs and error budgets, but onboarding a new service still takes three weeks. The CIO asks whether to grow the SRE team or create a platform team. Advise, and say what would change your answer.

items: **Symptom** = **slow onboarding** and **missing self-service** → these are **platform engineering's** concerns
**Platform team offers**: **golden paths**, **standardised provisioning**, **lower cognitive load**, with **developers treated as customers**
**SRE keeps owning reliability**; the platform can make **SLO monitoring a default** for every new service
a.foot: **What would change it**: if the main problem were **frequent outages** or **missed SLOs** instead of slow onboarding → **growing SRE** would be the better answer.

q: A regulated firm requires secret scanning, dependency checks and policy checks for every service. Option A gives each team a checklist to run before release. Option B builds the checks into the platform's golden path. Choose one and give the trade-off.

items.t: **Option B = shifting down**: checks embedded as **automated guardrails** and **secure defaults**
sub: removes **repeated manual toil**
applies the rules **consistently**
makes the **compliant path the easiest** one
fits the **security plane** being **cross-cutting**

items.t: **Option A = shifting left**: checks happen **early**, but
sub: **every team carries the work**
compliance depends on **each team's discipline**

a.foot: **Trade-off**: B costs **platform investment up front**, and teams that **leave the golden path** still need a way to **show compliance**.

q: A bank's architecture group plans to give its teams (a) a shared code skeleton with abstract classes, (b) a utility code package for date and currency handling, and (c) a hosted environment exposing identity and payment services through APIs, which partners may also use. Classify each, and explain which one creates an ecosystem and what that obliges the bank to do.

items: **(a) Framework**: teams use it and it **dictates structure**
**(b) Library**: teams **call it where they choose**
**(c) Platform**: **hosted**, **accessed by APIs**, and **extensible by outside parties**

items.t: **Ecosystem: only (c)** → partners can build **complementary products** through its interfaces
sub: **Obliges the bank** to keep those **interfaces stable** so **internal change does not break partners**
**Obliges the bank** to architect for **availability**, **security** and **scalability**

q: The Purchase client and the Purchase service both need the same Order entity classes, and the Purchase and Delivery services both need customer details. Which kind of reusable asset fits each need?

items: **Order entities** → a **shared library** used by the Purchase client and service → **reuse of classes** at a **small scale**
**Customer details** → a **Customer service** that Purchase and Delivery both call → **reuse of a business capability** across features
a.foot: Each choice has a cost: the **library ties client and service releases together**; the **service adds a remote call**.

q: A platform team must build ten new services quickly, all with the same web conventions, configuration and request handling. Should it reuse a service, a framework or a shared library?

a.lead: **A framework**, such as **Spring Boot** in the lecture.
items: **Framework** → reused to **build many clients and services**, giving them a **common structure and behaviour**
**Not a service** → provides a **capability at runtime**, not a way to build services
**Not a library** → supplies **classes** without **imposing the overall structure**
a.foot: **Catch**: a good framework is **expensive to design** → pays off only when **many services** will use it.

q: A proposed Customer service can scale only when the Order service scales with it, because the two share an in-process session cache. Which reusable-service characteristic does this break, and what would you change?

items: **Breaks**: **horizontal scalability without depending on other services**, and **loose coupling**
**Change**: give each service **its own state**; talk through its **interface** or **messages** (the lecture's **loosest coupling**)
a.foot: **Cost**: some **duplicated data** and accepting **eventual consistency** between the two.

q: A team used DDD to find well-bounded services, but each release still takes a week of manual packaging and deployment. A manager blames the domain design. Do you agree?

items: **DDD** produces designs that satisfy the **IDEALS** principles **except Deployability**
**Deployability** comes from **DevOps automation** of **packaging and deployment** → fix is **pipelines, not boundaries**
a.foot: The manager would have a point only if the boundaries force several services to be **released in lockstep** → that is a **coupling problem** in the design.

q: In a code review, a domain entity class imports the database driver and saves itself. Which onion-architecture rule does this break, and why does it matter for a reusable service?

items: **Rule broken**: **dependencies must point toward the centre**
**Inner layers define interfaces**; **outer layers implement** them → the **application core** compiles and runs **without infrastructure**
**Fix** → define a **repository interface** in the core and implement it in the **outer layer**
**Why it matters** → the core can then be **tested** and **reused with a different store**
a.foot: **Cost**: one more **interface and adapter**.

q: While modelling a service with DDD, a team adds RetryPolicy and HttpClientWrapper classes to the domain model. Should these be there?

items: **DDD** focuses squarely on **domain objects** and leaves out **non-domain concerns**
**OOAD**, by contrast, would add **design and framework objects** in later stages
**Retry and HTTP handling** still need designing → in the **outer layers** around the domain model
**Mixing them in** → blurs the **ubiquitous language** and **ties the core to infrastructure**

q: You receive a 60-entity domain model for a new platform and two weeks to propose services. Do you start by designing aggregates or by drawing bounded contexts?

items: **Strategic design** = **coarse-grained**: divides the domain into **contexts**, sets each one's **ubiquitous language**, classifies **core and subdomains**
**Aggregates** = **tactical**, **fine-grained** clusters **inside one context**
**Aggregates first** → risks clusters that **cut across** what should be **separate contexts**
a.foot: **Revisit** the context boundaries once aggregate design shows where **invariants** really sit.

q: When a backlog item is committed to a sprint, the resource-management context must update team availability. A teammate proposes that resource management reads the core context's tables directly. What would you use instead, and why?

a.lead: Use a **domain event**, not direct table reads.
items: **Core publishes a domain event**, e.g. **BacklogItemCommitted**
**Resource management reacts** to it in its **own transaction**
**Why**: each context keeps its **own schema and model** → the core can **change its tables** without breaking a consumer
a.foot: **Price**: **eventual consistency** → availability is updated **shortly after** the commit, not in the same transaction.

q: An e-commerce firm wins business through its pricing and recommendation engine; identity, billing and notifications look like everyone else's. Which is the core domain, and what does that classification change in your design?

items: **Core domain**: **pricing and recommendation** → the context **critical to the business**
**Supporting or generic subdomains**: **identity**, **billing**, **notifications**

sub: where the model needs **the most refinement**
which **generic contexts** are candidates to **split out and reuse across systems**

q: Underwriting, Claims and Inspections all use the word 'Policy'. An architect proposes one canonical Policy entity shared by all three teams. Do you agree?

items: **Inside each bounded context**, **Policy** has a **specific meaning** and does **specific things**
**One shared entity** → must carry **every context's attributes and rules** → **coupled to all three teams**
**DDD** → **segregates** them into **separate models** with their **own ubiquitous language**, **translating at the boundaries**
a.foot: **Cost**: **business and technical people** must agree **explicitly** on what Policy means in each context.

q: Two teams share one repository and one database schema for the Claims bounded context, and both change its interfaces. What problems would you expect, and what does the lecture prescribe?

sub: **conflicting changes** to the model and interfaces
**unclear ownership**
**schema changes** from one team **breaking the other**
**one team per bounded context** (a team may own several)
a **separate repository** with **source, acceptance and unit tests** together
a **separate schema**
**interfaces defined by the owning team**

a.foot: If the context is **too big for one team**, the **boundary itself is probably wrong**.

q: Every new feature adds entities to one shared domain model. The test suite now takes hours and teams disagree about what 'Account' means. Diagnose the problem and propose a fix.

items: **Diagnosis: Big Ball of Mud** → **tangled models**, **blurred language**, **no explicit boundaries**
**Fix**: split the entities by **functional cohesion** into **bounded contexts**, each with **one ubiquitous language** → 'Account' can mean different things in different contexts
**Each context** → a **smaller test set**; can become the boundary for a **service**, **repository**, **schema** and **team**
a.foot: **Cost**: **integration work** between contexts that used to **share objects**.

q: A group of developers tries to find bounded contexts from the existing database schema alone, without domain experts. What is the risk?

items: **Schema reflects the current, possibly tangled, model** → tends to **reproduce the Big Ball of Mud** rather than the **business's own boundaries**
**Lecture requires domain experts** → their **mental model drives entity extraction**
**Developers** must **engage with business aspects** instead of being **consumed by technology**
a.foot: The schema is **useful evidence**, but boundaries should come from **iterating on a combined model** with the experts.

q: From the scenario 'the product owner commits a backlog item to a sprint only if it is scheduled for release and a quorum of team members approved', a junior developer makes Quorum an entity. Do you agree?

items: **Nouns are candidate entities**, but some nouns are **properties of an entity** (lecture warning)
**Quorum approval** here is a **pre-condition on the commitment** → model it as **part of the commitment rule**
a.foot: It would become an **entity** only if **individual approvals** must be **tracked and changed over time**.

q: A team records its ubiquitous language as a glossary document kept apart from the code and tests. What does the lecture's approach add?

items: **Restate the concrete scenarios** as **executable Given/When/Then specifications** → serve as **acceptance tests**
**Language stays tied to verifiable behaviour**, e.g. the backlog item **becoming committed** and the **BacklogItemCommitted event** being created
a.foot: A **separate glossary drifts** from the code without anyone noticing.

q: In the Scrum tool split, Discussion appears in both the core context and the collaboration context. A reviewer flags it as duplication to remove. How do you respond?

items: **Each bounded context** has its **own ubiquitous language and model** → the **same name** can **mean and do different things** in each
**Merging them** → recreates a **shared model** that **couples the core to collaboration** features
a.foot: What is needed is an **explicit mapping** between them wherever the two contexts **interact**.

q: Another product line also needs tenant billing with accounts and payments, which the Scrum tool already has in its billing context. What does the lecture's procedure suggest?

items: **Procedure**: **split a bounded context further** if the resulting contexts are **more reusable across systems**
**Keep billing** as a **separate generic subdomain** with **no dependency on project-management concepts** → the other product can **reuse** it
a.foot: The billing context then needs a **stable interface** and an **owner who serves both consumers**.

q: A teammate proposes merging MaidOrderManager and MaidLoanManager into a single ServiceOrderManager, because both have plans, usages and bills. Do you agree?

items: **Different business functions**: **customer orders** vs **agency-to-agency loans**, with **different parties and plans**

sub: **Customers**: **OnceAFortnight**, **OnceAWeek**, **TwiceAWeek**
**Loans**: **Weekly**, **Monthly**
**MaidUsage** and **MaidUsagePlan**
against **MaidLoanUsage** and **MaidLoanPlan**

items: **Merged context** → would **change for two unrelated reasons** and **blur those terms**
a.foot: **Cost** of keeping them apart: some **parallel structure**.

q: Maid2Order adds a new digital-wallet payment method. Using the lecture's sample solution, which contexts change, and which should not?

items: **Changes: only PaymentManager** → add a new **ElectronicPayment** specialisation alongside **BankTransfer**, **PayNow** and **CreditCardPayment**, still producing a **Receipt**
**Unchanged**: **BillingManager**, **MaidOrderManager**, **MaidLoanManager** → they deal with **bills**, and a payment simply **settles a Bill**
a.foot: If they did need to change, that would show the **payment details had leaked across the boundary**.

q: A teammate proposes moving MaidUsageBill, MaidLoanBill and PlatformMonthlyBill into BillingManager so that every bill type lives in one place. Do you agree?

items: **Each specific bill** belongs to the **context whose business activity produces it**
**BillingManager** holds only the **common Bill** they lead to
**Pulling the specific types in** → BillingManager **depends on ordering, loan and platform-usage rules** → **changes whenever they do** and **cannot be reused** elsewhere
a.foot: **Cost** of the lecture's design: a **translation** from each specific bill to **Bill** at the boundary.

q: In the sample solution, Customer in CustomerManager holds only the customer's particulars. Where should the customer's current usage plan live, and why?

a.lead: In **MaidOrderManager**, as a **MaidUsage** under a **MaidUsagePlan** that **refers to the customer**.
items: **Why**: **ordering** is that context's responsibility → **CustomerManager stays small and reusable**
**The two contexts are linked by a reference**, not a **shared object**
a.foot: **Cost**: a screen showing both needs **data from two services**.

q: A platform's web, mobile, backend and partner services are built by different teams, each with its own way of calling the others and handling errors. What problem does this create, and what does the lecture recommend?

items: **Problem**: **inconsistent interactions** → every pair of systems needs **custom integration**, and the **same behaviour is rebuilt** many times
**Lecture recommends**: the **platform provider** uses **frameworks** to **standardise common behaviours** and the **interactions between services and clients**
a.foot: **Cost**: the **design effort** of the framework and **less freedom** for teams with unusual needs.

q: A ministry plans for each agency to build its own citizen-facing services and infrastructure, since each serves a different group. Using the SGTS case, argue against this, and say what is given up.

sub: **duplicate effort**
**inconsistent experience** for citizens
hard to **exchange data across agencies**

items.t: **SGTS**: a **common platform** of tools and services on **common infrastructure** → agencies:
sub: **build faster**
give a **more secure, consistent and connected experience**
get **easier data exchange** for **policy insights**

a.foot: **Given up**: agencies lose some **freedom** and **depend on the central platform's roadmap and availability**.

q: Users of your framework fall into two groups: beginners who want one call to send a payment, and experts who need control over retries and the wire format. How do you serve both?

items: **Lower layer** → **rich, low-level types**, exposes **all the power**
**Higher layer** → wraps it in **convenient calls** for the **common case**
**Result** → **simple things simple, complex things possible**, which a **single-layer API** cannot do
a.foot: **Cost**: designing and keeping **two consistent layers**.

q: A three-person team is building a framework for its own applications; a 20-person team is building one for external partners. Which framework-design process model fits each?

items.t: **Small team** (three people, own applications) → the model in which designers **alternate**
sub: between **building applications on the framework**
and **consolidating good extensions**
provided they can **budget effort for revision**

items.t: **Larger group targeting external users** (20 people, partners) → the **more popular** model
sub: **designers design and test**
**application builders extend it** and **give feedback**
**designers revise**

a.foot: That model only works if designers have **enough time set aside for the revisions**.

q: Partners are pressing for a framework, and the team wants to publish v1 to all of them after one internal application has used it. Advise.

items: **One application** is unlikely to be **representative**
**Publishing while the design is still changing** → **unstable interfaces ripple** into every partner's code
**Instead**: validate through a **few small pilot projects**; **release once suggestions for improvement become rare**
a.foot: Partners **wait longer** but **avoid painful rework**, and **'you can always add, you cannot ever remove'** argues against shipping **half-finished parts** just to have them.

q: A design review finds that one module of the framework names things and handles errors differently from the rest. Why is this a concern, and when could it be justified?

items: **Consistency** across the framework → promotes **productivity** and lets **knowledge transfer** from one part to another
**A deviation signals** that the part is **genuinely different**
**Accidental inconsistency** → sends that signal **falsely** → **confuses users**
a.foot: **Justified only** when the module really has a **unique consideration** → then the difference should be **deliberate and documented**.

q: To obey DRY, a teammate proposes a common-domain library of Customer, Order and Payment classes used by all 12 services. Do you agree?

items: **Shared domain library couples every service** to it → **one change** forces **coordinated changes and redeployments** across all **12**
→ undermines **independent release** and **blurs bounded contexts**
**Lecture's rule**: **don't violate DRY within a service**; be **relaxed about DRY across services**
a.foot: **Price**: some **duplicated code**, which is cheaper than **lockstep releases**.

q: Your platform will publish client libraries for its APIs. Option A: the API team writes a smart client that handles discovery, failures and logging, and all callers must use it. Option B: thin SDKs maintained separately, with callers choosing when to upgrade. Choose.

a.lead: **Option B** for a platform with **varied consumers**.
items: **Option B**, like the **AWS SDKs** → keeps clients **loosely coupled** to the server; they **upgrade on their own schedule**

sub: gets clients running **quickly and reliably**
but **couples them tightly**, **invites server logic into the client**
and **limits technology choices** if it is **mandated**

a.foot: **A** could suit a **single organisation** on **one technology stack** that values **uniform resilience**.

q: After a fix to a shared library, three services that did not need the fix have to be rebuilt and redeployed, and a Python client cannot use the library at all. Which drawbacks are these, and what would reduce them?

items: **Drawback 1**: a **new library version** cannot be deployed **without redeploying the whole process**
**Drawback 2**: the library is **language-specific** → **technology heterogeneity is lost**
**Shared communication code** = a **coupling point**, much like **regenerated RMI stubs**

sub: **not sharing code across service boundaries**
**separating transport-protocol code** from **service-specific code**
**letting clients decide when to upgrade**

q: The team that owns the Order service also writes its client library, and order-validation rules have started to appear in the library. What is the risk?

items: **Server logic creeping into the client library** → especially likely when the **same team owns both** (lecture)
**Server's cohesion breaks down**
**Fixing a rule** → changing and **rolling out many clients** instead of **one service**
a.foot: **Fix**: keep the **rules in the service**; limit the library to **making calls convenient**.

q: A ride-hailing platform's NotificationService defines every notification type itself, including TripAssigned, FareReceipt, DriverPayoutReady and PromoOffer, each with content specific to another service's responsibility. The company wants to reuse it in its new food-delivery platform without major adaptation. Identify the most likely cause of poor reusability, propose a countermeasure by revising the domain model, and give its main drawback.

items.t: **Cause**: the service is **not cohesive or single-minded**
sub: holds knowledge that belongs to the **Trip**, **Payment**, **Payout** and **Marketing** contexts
→ **coupled to this platform's domain**

items.t: **Countermeasure**: make it a **generic subdomain** that models only **generic concepts**
sub: e.g. a **notification** with **recipient**, **channel**, **template** and **delivery status**
move each specific notification's **content** into the **context that owns the event**
that context **requests sending** through a **published interface** or by **publishing domain events**
every **owning service** now has to **compose its own notifications**
**more integration** and some **repeated formatting code** across services

q: A logistics company has one shared model in which 'Shipment' means a customer order in Sales, a truck load in Dispatch and a customs declaration in Compliance. One team of 25 owns the code and a single database. Propose a restructuring of contexts, teams, repositories and data, and name one new problem it creates.

items.t: **Contexts**: split into **Sales**, **Dispatch** and **Compliance** bounded contexts, each with its **own ubiquitous language**
sub: 'Shipment' gets a **precise meaning** in each, e.g. **Order**, **Load** and **Declaration**
or the **same name** with **separate models**
**one owning team**
its **own repository** with **code** and **acceptance and unit tests**
its **own schema**
**interfaces defined by that team**

items: **Integration**: through **explicit interfaces** or **domain events**, **not shared tables**
**New problem**: a change that **spans contexts** needs **coordination and translation** between models → **eventual consistency** instead of **one local transaction**

q: In the Scrum tool, the product owner commits a backlog item to a sprint; it must already be scheduled for release, a quorum must approve, and if it is in another sprint it must be uncommitted first. Write the Given/When/Then specification, identify the aggregate or aggregates involved, and say how both sprints learn about the change.

sub: **Given** a backlog item **scheduled for release**, its **product owner**, a **target sprint** and **quorum approval**
**When** the product owner **commits** it to the sprint
**Then** it is **committed to the sprint** and a **BacklogItemCommitted** event is created
the **commitment rule** sits with it, as the aggregate whose **invariant** it is
the **sprint** is **referenced**, not changed in the **same transaction**

items.t: **How both sprints learn**: the **previous sprint** and the **new sprint** react to the **domain event**
sub: keeps each **transaction small**
but makes their views **eventually consistent**

a.foot: The scenario wording also becomes part of the context's **ubiquitous language** and doubles as an **acceptance test**.

q: Maid2Order adds corporate customers: a company subscribes to maid services for several offices and wants one monthly invoice. Using the lecture's seven-context solution, place the new concepts, justify each placement, and name one context that should not change.

items: **Corporate customer and its offices** → **CustomerManager**, as a **kind of Customer** → that context holds the **party's particulars**
**Per-office services** → stay in **MaidOrderManager** as **MaidUsage** under **usage plans** → **ordering rules** live there
**Single monthly invoice** → **BillingManager** → its **common Bill** can **consolidate the usage bills**
**Should not change: PaymentManager** → it simply **settles a Bill**
a.foot: If **corporate contracts** turn out to have **very different rules**, a **separate context** may be justified, at the cost of **more integration**.

q: A platform's 15 services all need (a) customer-profile lookups, (b) the same request logging, tracing and configuration conventions, and (c) a Money value class. Choose service, framework or shared library for each, and state the risk of each choice.

sub: **reuse of a business capability**, **scaled and released independently**
**Risk**: **remote-call latency and failures** → callers need **timeouts**
**standardises common behaviour** for **building many services**
**Risk**: **expensive to design well**; **ties services to its release cycle**
for a **small, stable value class**
**Risk**: **coupling** and **language lock-in** → share only **stable technical types**; keep **domain models within each service**

q: A four-person platform team must deliver an integration framework for 30 partner companies in nine months. Propose the design process and the qualities you would check, and name the pitfall you fear most.

sub: **analyse example integrations** from **several representative partners**
**design scenario-first** from **sample client code**
build a **whitebox** version for them
**pilot** it with **two or three partners**, **collect feedback** (the **external-user process model**)
make the framework **more blackbox**
**release widely** only when **suggestions become rare**
**simplicity**, **low barrier of entry**, **self-documenting names**
a **layered design** for **power users**
**consistency**, **testability**, **backward compatibility**

items.t: **Biggest pitfall**: **premature release** under **schedule pressure** with **unrepresentative examples**
sub: **unstable interfaces** would then **ripple into 30 partners' code**

q: A bank exposes each table of its core system as its own API and calls the job done. Six months later almost nobody uses them. Diagnose the problem.

a.lead: **Inside-out design**: the APIs expose existing resources rather than what consumers need → developers find them hard to use or not useful.
items: **Outside-in strategy**: start from the needs of developers and end users
Launch an **MVP**
Measure success by **adoption** and **business impact** through **usage analytics**
**API as a product**: the bank should treat the APIs as a product with an **owner** who iterates on that feedback

q: An API team is disbanded the week after launch because 'the project is delivered'. What goes wrong over the next year?

items: Nobody acts on **usage analytics** or **developer feedback** → the API **stops improving**
**Versions**, **documentation** and **endpoint stability** no longer managed → consumers meet **breaking changes** and **stale docs**
a.foot: The lecture's point: manage APIs as **products, not projects**: a **product owner** keeps a **backlog** from feedback and matures the API through **iterations**.

q: A single endpoint, /process-customer, creates a customer, opens an account and sends a welcome pack in one call. A partner only needs to create customers. Critique the design.

a.lead: Breaks the **granularity principles**: one API with several responsibilities.
items: Forces the partner to depend on behaviour it does not use → against **single responsibility** and **interface segregation**
**Design at the lowest practical level**: separate **customer** and **account** resources → consumers can combine them in different ways
a.foot: Trade-off: clients that need all three steps now make **more calls**, which a **composite at the gateway** can hide if needed.

q: A platform publishes its API with only a Java SDK and a custom binary protocol. Which design principle does this break, and what would you change?

a.lead: Breaks **ubiquitous standards**: develop APIs on **well-accepted standards** and make **no assumptions about the consumer's technology**.
items: Custom protocol + one SDK → **excludes consumers** on other stacks and slows **adoption**
**Fix**: expose a standard protocol such as **HTTP with JSON** and maintain **SDKs for several technologies**
a.foot: Cost: more SDKs to maintain.

q: An API keeps each user's session in the memory of the instance that served the login, so the load balancer uses sticky sessions. Traffic triples during a sale and one instance crashes. What goes wrong, and what does REST's stateless constraint suggest?

items: **Sessions lost**: users pinned to the crashed instance lose their sessions
**Uneven load**: requests must return to their own instance → load cannot be spread evenly
**Statelessness**: the **client holds the application state** and **each request carries its own context**
→ **any instance can serve any request** → scale by **adding instances**, with no server-side **session synchronisation**
a.foot: Persistent resource data still needs a **shared store**.

q: An API runs on eight instances, each with an in-process cache of product prices. Users see different prices depending on which instance answers. Diagnose the problem and propose a fix.

a.lead: Each **in-process cache is local to its instance** → updates reach the caches at different times.
items: **Fix: distributed cache** → consistent across requests to multiple servers
Survives **restarts and deployments**
a.foot: Trade-off: **slower than local memory**, another service to run, and still needs a policy for **invalidating stale entries**.

q: Pick an API style for (a) in-app chat, (b) telling a partner system the moment a file upload completes, and (c) a mobile dashboard whose data needs vary by screen. Justify each choice.

items: **(a) WebSocket**: continuous **two-way real-time** messages
**(b) Webhook**: an **event notification** that calls the partner when the upload happens → the partner does not have to **poll**
**(c) GraphQL**: each screen asks for **exactly the fields** it needs in **one request**
a.foot: These match the lecture's typical uses; a **REST** API could still serve (c) if **HTTP caching** matters more than flexible queries.

q: A reviewer says your API is not RESTful because the server never sends scripts for the client to run. Do you agree?

a.lead: **No.** **Code on demand** is the one REST constraint that is **not strictly required**.
items: It lets the server **extend a client by sending code** → reduces what the client must pre-implement
**Required constraints**: **client-server**, **stateless**, **uniform interface**, **layered system**, **caching**
a.foot: Review the API against the required ones instead.

q: Critique this orders API and rewrite it: POST /createOrder; GET /orders/delete?id=9; PUT /orders with the new order in the body; GET /getCustomers?customer-id=7&orders-id=9; GET /products/sort/price/page/2.

items: **Plural nouns, no verbs**: POST /orders to create (**201**)
**GET must be safe** → deletion becomes DELETE /orders/9
**PUT updates a known resource** → PUT /orders/9 or PATCH /orders/9
**Path variables** for identity and relationships → GET /customers/7/orders/9
**Query parameters** only to shape results → GET /products?sort=price&page=2&limit=50
a.lead: Resources should be plural nouns; fix each call:

q: A mobile client times out on POST /payments and retries. How do you make sure the customer is not charged twice?

items: **Idempotency key**: generate one for the intended payment and send the **same key on every retry**
Server **records the key with the outcome** → on a repeat, returns the **recorded result** without charging again
a.foot: Pitfalls: generating a **fresh key per attempt** defeats the protection; the server must **keep keys** long enough to cover the **retry window**.

q: A client times out on DELETE /orders/9, retries, and gets 404. A developer fears the retry did harm. Did it?

items: **Idempotency concerns server state**: after one or several calls the order is gone either way
Only the **response** differs: typically **204** then **404**
a.foot: The client should treat a **404 on a retried delete** as 'already deleted'.

q: A cart API offers PATCH /carts/5/items/3 with either {"quantity": 5} or {"increment": 1}. The client library retries PATCH automatically on timeout. Is that safe?

items: **Setting quantity to 5**: leaves the **same state** however often it repeats
**Incrementing by 1**: adds **another item on every retry**
**PATCH is not guaranteed to be idempotent**
a.foot: Fix: either disable **automatic retries** for the increment or protect it with an **idempotency key**.

q: An API returns 200 with the body {"error": "customer not found"} for unknown customers, and 500 when the client sends malformed JSON. What is wrong, and what should it return?

a.lead: Return **404** for the missing customer and **400** for the malformed request.
items: **Status codes tell the developer who behaved wrongly**: **4xx** = the client did, **5xx** = the API did
**As built**: clients cannot handle errors from the status code
**Monitoring** raises server alarms for client mistakes while **missing real failures**

q: A clerk with a valid token calls DELETE /accounts/7, which only managers may do, and the API returns 401. Is that the right code?

a.lead: **No, it should be 403**: the credentials were accepted, but the caller **lacks permission** for this resource.
items: **401** = credentials **missing or not recognised** → the client may try to **log in again**, which cannot help
**Clear codes** improve **developer experience** → API easier to **adopt**

q: Since this morning's release, 2% of requests return 500. A developer proposes changing code directly on a production server to test a theory. How do you respond?

a.lead: **Don't**: blind changes in production are the lecture's **'big mistake'** → they can **widen the outage** and leave **no audit trail**.
items: **Correlate logs, metrics and traces** to find the failing path
**Compare** against what the release changed, and **reproduce safely**
If the release is the cause → **roll back**, then ship a **verified fix** through the **normal pipeline**

q: A downstream dependency is down for planned maintenance for ten minutes. Should your API answer 500 or 503?

a.lead: **503 Service Unavailable**, ideally with a **retry header**.
items: **503** → tells clients the condition is **temporary**; a later retry may succeed
**500** = **generic server error** → invites **investigation** rather than a timed retry
a.foot: Clients still need **backoff** so they do not hammer the API when it comes back.

q: A booking API has one endpoint, POST /api, with bodies such as {"action": "getBooking", "id": 5} and {"action": "cancelBooking", "id": 5}. Which RMM level is it, and what changes would take it to level 2?

a.lead: **Level 0**: HTTP is only a **transport for RPC-style messages** → no resources and no HTTP semantics.
items: **Level 1**: each booking gets its own **URI**, /bookings/5

items.t: **Level 2**: then use the **verbs** and **status codes** properly
sub: **Read**: GET /bookings/5 (**200** or **404**)
**Cancel**: DELETE /bookings/5, or a **PATCH** of its status (**204**)

q: An API exposes GET /v1/rooms/{room-id} to read a room and GET /v1/rooms/{room-id}/book to make a booking. The team says it is level 2 because it has resources. Do you agree?

a.lead: **No**: it has resource URIs, which is only **level 1**.
items: Uses **GET for a state-changing action** and puts a **verb in the path** → does not use HTTP verbs as **level 2** requires
**GET must be safe**: caches, crawlers or retries could **create bookings by accident**
**Fix**: model bookings as a resource → POST /v1/rooms/{room-id}/bookings returning **201** with the new booking's **location**

q: A mobile client hard-codes 40 URL patterns and breaks whenever the server reorganises its URLs. Which RMM level addresses this, and what does it demand of the client?

items: Responses carry **hypermedia links** to related resources and next actions
→ the **server controls URL structure**; the client **discovers** it from responses
→ **looser coupling**; lets the API **evolve**
a.foot: Demand on the client: it must be written to **follow links instead of building URLs**, and responses get somewhat **larger**.

q: A teammate says moving the API from RMM level 2 to level 3 will raise its throughput under load. Do you agree?

items: **RMM grades** how fully an API uses **resources**, **HTTP semantics** and **hypermedia**
The lecture links higher levels with **scalability** and **evolvability** through **looser coupling** and **cacheable, uniform interfaces**
But **adding links** does not by itself make requests **faster**
a.foot: **Throughput** has to be shown with **load tests**.

q: A mobile screen needs a customer, their last five orders and the product names, which now takes three REST calls over slow networks. Separately, a public product catalogue is read millions of times a day through HTTP caches. Would you use GraphQL for both?

a.lead: **No**: use **GraphQL** for the mobile screen and **REST** for the catalogue.
items: **Mobile screen → GraphQL**: one query to one endpoint returns exactly those fields → avoids **over- and under-fetching** across three calls
**Catalogue → keep REST**: resource URLs and standard **HTTP caching** serve repeated identical reads cheaply
**GraphQL queries are hard to cache** in web caches
a.foot: Cost: running **two styles**, justified by two different **access patterns**.

q: A team implements 'place order' as a GraphQL query because the call returns the new order. Critique this.

a.lead: Placing an order **changes data** → it should be a **mutation**; **queries are for reading**.
items: As a query it **misleads clients and tools** that treat queries as **safe to repeat or cache**
→ an **automatic retry** could place a **second order**
**Subscriptions** are the third operation type: **pushing updates** as they happen, such as order status changes

q: Team A writes the API code first and generates documentation afterwards. Team B agrees an OpenAPI description with consumers before writing code. What does B's design-first approach buy, and what does it cost?

items: **Separates the interface from the backend implementation** → consumers can **review and build against the contract early**
**Documentation matches the API** from the start
**OpenAPI** is a **vendor-neutral standard format** → tools and consumers on any stack can use it
a.foot: Cost: **upfront agreement time**, and the contract must then be **kept in sync** with the code.

q: Your API is at version 2.4.1. Give the new version for each change: (a) an optional 'notes' field is added to the order response; (b) 'amount' is renamed to 'total'; (c) a rounding bug is fixed without changing the contract.

items: **(a) 2.5.0**: a backward-compatible feature → bumps the **minor** version
**(b) 3.0.0**: renaming a field **breaks existing consumers** → the **major** version goes up
**(c) 2.4.2**: a backward-compatible fix → bumps the **patch**
a.foot: Change (b) also needs **version 2 kept available** for a while, because the rules say **not to take anything away abruptly**.

q: An API puts its full version in every URI, such as /v1.1/orders, and changes the URI for every minor release, so all consumers must update their URLs each time. Propose a better strategy.

items: Put just the **major version** in the URI (/v1/orders) or move it to an **Accept** or **custom header**
Make **minor and patch** releases **backward compatible** → the URIs consumers call stay the same
Keep the **old major version running** with an **explicit service level** while consumers migrate
a.foot: **URI versioning** is visible and easy to test; **header versioning** keeps URIs stable but is harder to see and to try in a browser.

q: A field is deprecated and only 3% of calls still use it. The team wants to delete it next week. What do the versioning rules say?

items: **Removal is a breaking change** → belongs in a **new major version**
The current version **keeps the field** under an **explicit service level**
The change is **announced** through the **developer portal**
a.foot: The **3%** may include an **important partner**, so check who they are before setting the **deadline**.

q: Each of 12 services currently implements its own token validation, rate limits and request validation, each slightly differently. What would you propose, and what must stay in the services?

a.lead: Put an **API gateway** in front as the **single gatekeeper**.
items: → **authentication**, **rate limits** and **schema validation** enforced **consistently** for every client
**Services must still authorise business actions**: a valid token does not prove permission on a particular resource
**Services must still validate the data they rely on**
a.foot: Risk: the gateway becomes a **critical component** and must be **highly available**.

q: An activity feed receives new items every second and pages with ?page=N&limit=50. Users scrolling down see duplicate items. Diagnose the problem and fix it.

a.lead: **Offset pagination drifts**: new items inserted at the top push earlier items onto the next page.
items: **Fix: cursor pagination** → ask for items **after the last one seen**
Use a **stable sort order** with a **unique tie-breaker**: a **timestamp alone** can skip or repeat items with equal times
a.foot: Cost: clients can no longer **jump straight to page 37**.

q: A client retries every failed call to a slow partner API five times immediately. During a partner outage, the partner receives six times its normal traffic and the client's threads are exhausted. What would you change?

items: **Timeout** → calls cannot wait indefinitely
**Retry with exponential backoff**
**Circuit breaker** in front of the partner → stops calling it after repeated failures and returns a **fallback**
**Bulkhead isolation** → keeps the partner's calls from using up **threads** needed for other work
a.foot: Trade-off: users get **degraded responses** during the outage instead of **eventual success**.

q: An operations lead proposes CPU usage as the main health metric for a public API. Does it show what users experience?

items: An API can **fail requests or respond slowly while CPU is low**, for example while waiting on a dependency
**Users experience** **latency**, **failure rate** and **uptime**

sub: **Application metrics**: requests per minute, latency, failure rate
**Infrastructure metrics**: uptime, memory and CPU

a.foot: CPU is still useful for **capacity planning**.

q: A tester checks performance by repeatedly sending requests from a manual API client on a laptop, then reports that the API 'handles load fine'. The target is 3 seconds for 90% of requests at 5,000 concurrent users. Do you accept the result?

items: **Manual requests from one laptop** → neither the **target concurrency** nor **repeatable conditions**
→ results vary with the laptop and network and say little about the **90th percentile**
**Fix**: run **automated load and stress tests** that generate the defined **concurrency and duration** from a **controlled environment**
Report **percentile latency** against the target
**Stress tests** then show **where the API breaks** beyond that load

q: An API passes all its functional tests and will be public from launch. What else would you check before production?

sub: **Deny by default**
**Least privilege**
**Rejecting illegal input**
**HTTPS only**
Correct **role permissions**
No **internal data leaking** into public responses
**Rate limiting**

items: **Performance**: **load and stress tests** against the expected traffic
**Usability** for developers
**Monitoring** in place for **latency** and **failure rate**
a.foot: Functional tests show that the **contract works**, not that the API is **safe or fast enough**.

q: Average responses are 2 KB of JSON, one report endpoint returns 3 MB of JSON, and the API also serves images. Where would you enable gzip?

a.lead: Enable it for the **large JSON report** and other **big text responses**.
items: There the **bandwidth saved** outweighs the **compression CPU**
**Skip small payloads**: the cost is not worth it
**Skip already-compressed content** such as **images**
a.foot: **Measure** response size and latency **before and after**, rather than turning it on everywhere.

q: A mobile list screen downloads full 40-field product objects to display three fields, and an edit screen sends the whole object with PUT to change one price. What would you change in each?

items: **List → partial response**: the server returns **only the requested fields** → cuts **payload** and **parsing time**
**Edit → PATCH** with only the fields to modify, plus any **enclosing parent objects**
a.foot: Two different tools: a **partial response** trims what the **server sends**, and **PATCH** trims what the **client sends**.

q: Match each need to OAuth, JWT or SAML: (a) a third-party budgeting app needs delegated access to a user's bank transactions; (b) staff already signed in to the corporate portal should reach a partner web app without logging in again; (c) the access token should carry the issuer, subject and expiry in a compact form.

items: **(a) OAuth**: the **authorisation framework** through which the client obtains an **access token** from an **authorisation server**
**(b) SAML**: a **single sign-on** standard that passes identity from an existing session using an **XML document**
**(c) JWT**: a **token format** that can be used inside OAuth
a.foot: A design note saying '**JWT instead of OAuth**' confuses a token format with the framework for obtaining tokens.

q: A browser web app gets a CORS error calling your API, but the same request works from a command-line client. What do you check?

sub: **origin**, **scheme**, **port**
**methods**, **headers** and **credentials**

items: The server can answer the **pre-flight request** without error
The **API gateway** relays the **pre-flight response** to the browser
a.foot: The command-line client works because **CORS is enforced only by browsers**.

q: A teammate proposes a strict CORS policy as the main protection for a payment API. Is that enough?

a.lead: **No.** **CORS** only controls whether a **browser** lets a page from another **origin** read the response.
items: **Scripts, servers** and other **non-browser clients** ignore it entirely
The API must still **authenticate and authorise each call**, **validate payloads** and apply **rate limits**

q: Your API receives a million requests a day, 30% of them with missing or null fields, and the application crashes on the nulls. How do you handle this in production?

items: **Validate requests against the API schema at the edge**: content, parameters and headers
**Reject bad ones with a 400** that explains which field is wrong
**Inside the service**: handle optional fields **defensively** → one bad request cannot **crash the process**
**Log and monitor the rejection rate**: **30%** suggests a **client bug** or a **confusing contract** worth fixing at the source

q: An Order service and an Inventory service have separate databases. At peak there are 2,000 orders a minute, and Inventory is sometimes slow. Would you use two-phase commit or a saga?

items: **Two-phase commit** holds **locks across both services** until both are ready → a slow Inventory **stalls every order** and **couples their availability**
**Saga**: each service **commits locally** and **publishes an event**
A failure triggers **compensation**, such as cancelling the order
a.foot: Trade-off: accept **eventual consistency**; must design **compensations** and **idempotent handlers**.

q: In the lecture's centrally directed saga, Inventory replies 'Failed to Reserve Items'. What happens next, and why is this orchestration even though messages go through an event bus?

items: **Next**: the **coordinator** sends a **compensating 'Delete Order'** to undo the order already committed, and **notifies the user**
**Orchestration** because **one coordinator decides the next step**; the **event bus is only the transport**
In **choreography**, each service would **react to the failure event on its own**

q: A mobile app calls six microservices directly, each with its own address, authentication scheme and response format. What problems does this cause, and what does an API gateway fix?

sub: The app is **coupled** to each service's **location and contract**
Makes **many round trips**
Has to handle **six security schemes**
→ every internal change risks **breaking a released app**
**One entry point** with **central security** and **routing**
Can **compose several calls** into one response
Lets services **move or split** behind it

a.foot: Cost: it adds a **hop** and a component that must be **highly available**.

q: A clinic platform's first two APIs are designed as follows. API 1: URI /v2.3/appointments/{patient-id}/book, service BookingManager, input the patient id, output the list of all doctors, HTTP verb GET. API 2: URI /v2.3/appointments/{patient-id}/cancel, service BookingManager, inputs the patient id and patient name, output the list of all patients' appointments, HTTP verb GET. (1) Do they comply with RMM level 2? (2) Propose a versioning strategy that affects consumers less. (3) Give corrected interfaces.

sub: Resource-like URIs → only **level 1**
But GET is used for **state-changing actions** and **verbs sit in the path**, so HTTP verbs aren't used as **level 2** requires
**GET must be safe**
Only the **major version** in the URI (/v2) or in a **header**
Keep **minor and patch** releases **backward compatible** → consumers unaffected by them
**Book**: POST /v2/patients/{patient-id}/appointments; inputs doctor id and time slot → **201** + the created appointment with its **location**
**Cancel**: DELETE /v2/patients/{patient-id}/appointments/{appointment-id}, or **PATCH** its status to cancelled → **204** or the updated appointment
Drop the **redundant patient name** and the unrelated lists of **all doctors** or **all appointments**

q: Design a RESTful API for a cleaning-service platform. Customers make one-off orders or subscribe to OnceAFortnight, OnceAWeek or TwiceAWeek plans, change or cancel subscriptions, and pay; the mobile app retries on timeouts. Give resources, verbs and status codes, and explain how you handle retries.

sub: /customers/{customer-id}/orders: **POST** creates a one-off order (**201**); **GET** lists orders with ?status= and **pagination**
/plans: **GET**
/customers/{customer-id}/subscriptions: **POST** subscribes (**201**); **PATCH** /subscriptions/{subscription-id} changes the plan (**200** or **204**); **DELETE** cancels (**204**)
/payments: **POST** (**201**)

items: **Naming**: plural **kebab-case nouns**, no verbs, **path variables** for identity and **query parameters** for filtering
**Retries**: retried POSTs to orders, subscriptions and payments carry an **idempotency key** → the server returns the **recorded outcome** for a repeat
**Maturity**: aim for **level 2**; add links (**level 3**) such as a subscription's **cancel** and **change-plan** links if clients would benefit
**Versioning**: version as /v1

q: A published API at version 1 has 200 partner integrations. You must split 'name' into 'firstName' and 'lastName', add an optional loyalty-points field, and fix a currency-rounding bug. Plan the releases and the partner impact.

items: **Bug fix → patch**; **optional loyalty field → minor** release: neither breaks partners, so they need **no changes**

items.t: **Name split → version 2** (/v2 or a v2 **media type**)
sub: Changes meaning and **removes a field** → breaking
**Version 1 keeps returning 'name'** under an **explicit service level**

items: **Announce** the change and its **timeline** through the **developer portal**; **track v1 usage per partner** before retiring it
a.foot: Cost: running **two versions side by side** for the migration period.

q: A public payment API serves a browser single-page app and partner servers. It receives a million requests a day, 30% with malformed or null fields, and retried POSTs have caused some duplicate charges. Design its security and robustness, and name one drawback of your design.

sub: **TLS**
**OAuth 2.0 access tokens** (**JWT** is one possible format)
Per-client **rate limits** and **quotas**
**Schema validation** that rejects malformed requests with a **400**

items: **Services still authorise each action** and validate **business invariants**
Configure **CORS** for the single-page app's **origin only**, remembering that **CORS is not authentication**
Require an **idempotency key** on payment POSTs → retries return the **original result**
Add **timeouts**, **circuit breakers** on downstream calls, and **monitoring** of **latency** and **failure rate**
a.foot: **Drawback**: the gateway is a **critical shared component**, and strict validation will initially **reject many partner requests** until partners fix their clients.

q: After a release, the 95th-percentile latency of GET /orders rose from 300 ms to 4 seconds, while database query times are unchanged. Give the most likely causes, how you would confirm them, a fix, and the fix's drawback.

items.t: **Likely causes**: fast queries → the time is spent elsewhere
sub: A new or slower **downstream call**
A **thread or connection pool** being exhausted
**Larger payloads** from the release
**Distributed traces** to find the **slow span**
Then check **pool metrics** and the **release diff**

items.t: **Fix** (if a downstream call is the cause)
sub: Add a **timeout** and **circuit breaker** with a **fallback**
Or call it **in parallel**, or **cache** the result

items: **Drawback**: **degraded or slightly stale** responses when the fallback or cache is used → the change needs a **load test** before release

q: A product team must choose between REST and GraphQL for a mobile dashboard that aggregates data from six microservices; a public catalogue endpoint on the same platform is mostly anonymous, repeated reads. Recommend a style for each and give the trade-offs.

sub: **Client-driven**: one query to one endpoint fetches **exactly the fields** needed from several services
→ cuts mobile **round trips** and **over-fetching**
The **schema and type system** document the data
**Server-driven** and **resource-oriented**
Identical repeated reads benefit from ordinary **HTTP and CDN caching**, which GraphQL makes hard

a.foot: Cost: **two styles** to run and secure, plus **resolvers** that must call the six services efficiently.

q: A team splits a monolith by turning each in-process method call into a remote call one for one. A single page now makes 40 remote calls and is slow. Diagnose the problem.

a.lead: Remote calls **cost far more** than in-process calls → remote APIs need to be **coarser-grained** than the **library-style interfaces** they replaced.
items: Services should expose **fewer, larger operations** around **business capabilities**
May mean **revisiting the boundaries**
a.foot: Moving responsibilities between services later is **harder** once they sit across **process boundaries**, so the split deserves **care up front**.

q: Order and Inventory now own separate databases. A manager asks for 'one ACID transaction across both, like before'. How do you respond?

a.lead: Microservices favour **decentralised data**: each service manages its **own database** and coordinates with others **without a shared transaction**.
items: → **eventual consistency** plus **compensating operations**, such as **releasing stock** if the order fails
If the business truly needs both changes to **commit atomically** → that suggests the data **belongs in one service** rather than a **distributed transaction**

q: A company has separate UI, backend and database teams, and every new feature becomes a cross-team project needing budget approval. What does Conway's law predict about its system, and what would you change?

sub: Layers **owned by different teams**, **tangled together**
Logic pushed into whichever part a team can touch
Organise **cross-functional teams** around **business capabilities**, each with the **full range of skills** from **user experience** to **database**
→ each team's service **matches a capability**
Teams **own their service end to end**, including **running it**

q: An architect proposes putting routing, message transformation and business rules into a central message bus so the services can stay simple. Critique the proposal.

a.lead: That is the **enterprise-service-bus** style, with **smarts in the pipe**.
items: Microservices prefer **smart endpoints and dumb pipes**: the logic stays in **cohesive services** and the bus **only routes messages**
A smart central bus **couples every service** to **one shared component** and its team → changes **queue up** there
a.foot: Cost of the microservice style: each service **owns more of its own logic**.

q: Your small Shipping team must integrate with a large, established ERP whose team will not change anything for you. Should Shipping be a Conformist or build an Anticorruption Layer?

a.lead: **It depends** on whether Shipping's model can live with the ERP's.
items: **Conform** if it can, and the team cannot sustain the **effort of translating** → it is **cheaper**
**Build an Anticorruption Layer** if the ERP is a **Big Ball of Mud** that would **distort Shipping's model** → translates to Shipping's **ubiquitous language**
a.foot: ACL trade-off: accept the cost of **maintaining the translation**.

q: Eight downstream contexts each maintain their own translation of the Customer context's model, and every Customer change breaks several of them. What should the Customer team offer instead?

a.lead: An **Open Host Service** with a **Published Language**.
items: **Open Host Service**: a **protocol or set of services** giving access to the context
**Published Language**: such as a documented **JSON Schema**
→ downstream teams can **consume and translate easily**; an **anticorruption layer** becomes **less crucial** for them
a.foot: Cost: the Customer team takes on keeping that **public interface stable and versioned**.

q: Marketing wants a small piece of Billing's data, but Billing's model does not really provide what Marketing needs, and integrating would take months. What mapping fits?

items: Integration would **not give a significant payoff**: the functionality sought is **not fully provided** by the source **ubiquitous language**
Marketing builds its **own specialised solution**
a.foot: Cost: some **duplicated capability**, which is cheaper than **months of integration**.

q: Two teams propose a shared kernel of 40 classes so they can stop translating between their contexts. What concerns would you raise?

items: A **shared kernel** should be a **small common model**
Even then it is **hard to conceive and maintain**: needs **open communication** and **constant agreement** between both teams
**Forty classes** → would **bind their release schedules** together
a.foot: Alternative: a **Customer-Supplier** relationship, or an **Open Host Service** with a **Published Language**, keeps the teams more **independent**.

q: When an order is placed, the Loyalty context must add points. Loyalty is offline for 20 minutes every night for maintenance. Would you integrate with REST or messaging?

items: Order publishes a **domain event**; Loyalty **processes it when it comes back**
→ removes the **temporal coupling** of a **blocking REST call** that would fail or stall orders during the outage
Needs **at-least-once delivery** and an **idempotent receiver** in Loyalty
a.foot: Trade-off: points appear **later** rather than immediately.

q: After a broker redelivery, the Loyalty subscriber processes the same OrderPlaced event twice and awards double points. What is the fix?

a.lead: **At-least-once delivery** means redelivery is expected → the **receiver must be idempotent**.
items: **Record processed event IDs** and **skip duplicates**
Or make the update **safe to reapply**: 'set points for order X' instead of 'add points'
a.foot: Switching off redelivery would just swap **duplicates** for **lost messages**.
